resources.title: Adding & Subtracting Polynomials

content.topicNotes: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials Adding and subtracting polynomials can be thought of as just adding and subtracting like terms. Look for terms with the same variables with the same exponent. Identify like terms Identify like terms by underlining or circling like terms. Rearrange The commutative property of addition allows us to rearrange the terms in polynomials to put like terms together. Remember to keep track of any minus signs. Combine like terms Sum the coefficients of terms of the same degree to write the polynomial in its simplest form. Adding and Subtracting Polynomials To add or subtract polynomials, you must: Identify like terms Rearrange Combine like terms

resources.title: Algebraic Long Division

content.topicNotes: The Division Algorithm The division of polynomials that contain more than one term is similar to the long division of whole numbers. Set up the division Step 1 Divide $$2x^3$$ by $$x$$ to give $$2x^2$$. Write $$2x^2$$ on top of the division in line with the $$x^2$$ term of the polynomial. Step 2 Multiply $$(x+2)$$ by $$2x^2$$ to give $$ 2x^3 + 4x^2$$. Subtract $$2x^3+4x^2$$ from $$2x^3-3x^2$$ to give $$-7x^2$$.. The highest-order terms will always cancel out. Write the resulting term of order $$x^2$$ underneath. Step 3 Divide $$-7x^2$$ by $$x$$ to give $$-7x$$. Write this above the division line. Step 4 Bring down the next term in the polynomial. Step 5 Multiply $$x+2$$ by $$-7x$$ and subtract this from $$-7x^2+4x$$. Step 6 Divide $$18x$$ by $$x$$ to give $$18$$. Write this above the division line. Step 7 Bring down the final term of the polynomial. Step 8 Multiply $$x+2$$ by $$18$$ and subtract this from $$18x+5$$. -31 is the remainder of the division. Step 8 Answer The quotient is the polynomial that is written above the division, and the remainder is the constant left over.

resources.title: Angle Addition Formulae

content.topicNotes: Angle Addition Formulae Finding the exact value of the sine, cosine, or tangent of an angle is often easier if we can rewrite the given angle in terms of two angles that have known trigonometric values. Sine We can write the sine of the sum of two angles $$A$$ and $$B$$ using the following identity: $$\sin(A+B) \equiv \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B$$ We can write the cosine of the sum of two angles $$A$$ and $$B$$ using the following identity: $$\cos(A+B) \equiv \cos A\cos B -\sin A\sin B$$ Proof Consider two right-angled triangles stacked on top of each other as shown. The upper triangle (triangle 1) has a hypotenuse equal to 1, with the left corner angle equal to $$A$$ The lower triangle (triangle 2) has a left corner angle equal to $$B$$ Label triangle 1 Using the fact that the hypotenuse is 1 and the left corner angle is $$A$$, we can label the sides of the upper triangle using trigonometry: Adjacent = hypotenuse $$\times\cos(\text{angle}) = \cos A$$ Opposite = hypotenuse $$\times\sin(\text{angle}) = \sin A$$ Label triangle 2 Using the fact that the hypotenuse is $$\cos A$$ and the left corner angle is $$B$$, we can label the sides of the lower triangle using trigonometry: Adjacent = hypotenuse $$\times\cos(\text{angle})= \cos A\cos B $$ Opposite = hypotenuse $$\times\sin(\text{angle})=\cos A\sin B$$ Triangle 3 Notice that the hypotenuse of triangle 1 forms another right-angled triangle with angle $$A+B$$. By trigonometry: Adjacent = $$\cos(A+B)$$ Opposite = $$\sin(A+B)$$ Find angles of triangle 4 Triangle 4 is formed by the opposite side of triangle 1 as shown. By alternate angle theorem, the angle beneath triangle 4 is equal $$B$$. This means the right corner angle of triangle 4 is equal to 90 $$- B$$. So the top corner angle is equal to $$B$$. Find sides of triangle 4 The hypotenuse of triangle 4 is $$\sin A$$. By trigonometry: Opposite = hypotenuse $$\times \cos(\text{angle}) = \sin A \cos B$$ Adjacent = hypotenuse $$\times \sin(\text{angle}) = \sin A \sin B$$ Find opposite side of triangle 3 The length of the opposite side of triangle 3 is equal to: Opposite = $$\sin(A+B) = \sin A \cos B + \cos A\sin B$$ Which is the angle addition formula for sine. Find adjecent side of triangle 3 The length of the adjacent side of triangle 3 is equal to: Opposite = $$\cos(A+B) = \cos A \cos B - \sin A\sin B$$ Which is the angle addition formula for cosine.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Trigonometry > Trigonometric Identities

resources.title: Arc length

content.topicNotes: Arc Length of a Sector We can find the arc length of a sector of a circle given the radius of the circle and the angle of the sector. Arc length The length of the arc of a sector of a circle is equal to the radius $$r$$ multiplied by the angle θ: $$s = r\theta$$ Where the angle θ is measured in radians. Example What is the arc length, $$s$$, of the sector with angle $$\theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}$$ radians and radius 4.5 cm? Arc length The equation for arc length is $$s = r\theta$$. Substituting in, we get: $$s = 4.5 \times \frac{2\pi}{5} = \frac{9\pi}{5} = 5.65$$ cm (2 d.p.)

resources.title: Area of Sectors

content.topicNotes: Area of a Sector of a Circle As with the arc length, we can also use angles to find the area of a sector of a circle. Derivation The area of a circle with radius $$r$$ is equal to $$\pi r^2$$. If the sector angle is $$\theta$$ radians, then $$\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$$ is the sector angle as a fraction of the angle in a full circle. This means the area of the sector as a fraction of the area of the circle must also be equal to $$\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$$. Derivation cont. So the area of a sector is equal to: $$\frac{\small A}{\small \pi r^2} = \frac{\small \theta}{\small 2\pi} \rightarrow A= \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$$ Example What is the area of a sector of a circle with radius 6 cm and angle $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$$ rad? Area of sector The area of a sector is $$A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$$. Substituting in, we have: $$A = \frac{1}{2}\times6^2\times\frac{\pi}{4} = 4.5\pi = 14.14$$ cm2

resources.title: Area of Segments

content.topicNotes: Area of a Segment of a Circle We can use the area of a sector as well as the area of a triangle to find the area of a segment of a circle. Derivation A sector of a circle of radius $$r$$ and angle $$\theta$$ has points A and B on the circumference of the circle. AB forms a segment of the circle. The area of the segment is given by: Area of segment = area of sector − area of triangle ABC. Derivation cont. The area of a triangle is equal to $$\frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$, which for ABC, is equal to: $$\frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta$$ The area of the segment is then equal to: Area of segment = $$\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta - \frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$$ Example What is the area of the shaded segment formed by the line $$PQ$$? Area of segment The area of the segment is equal to $$\frac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$$. Substituting in, we have: Area of segment = $$\frac{1}{2}\times4^2\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\times16\times0.0235...$$ Area of segment = 0.19 cm2

resources.title: Area of a Triangle

content.topicNotes: Area of a Triangle We can use the formula: area of a triangle = 1⁄2ab sin(C). Formula Area of a triangle = 1⁄2ab sin(C) since the vertical height is b sin(C). This formula can also be used to calculate the side length of a triangle whose area is known. Example If we are given a triangle with two sides of 8cm and 10cm and the area is 20cm2, we can calculate the angle between the sides as follows: 20 = 1⁄2 × 8 × 10 × sin(C) 20 = 40 × sin(C) sin(C) = 1⁄2 C = 30°

resources.title: Arithmetic Sequences

content.topicNotes: Arithmetic Sequence Terms in arithmetic sequences change by a constant amount each time. Arithmetic sequence An arithmetic sequence is a sequence that has the property that the difference between any two consecutive terms is a constant. This difference is called the common difference, and is represented by the symbol $$d$$. Explicit formula Given the first term and the common difference of an arithmetic sequence, we can find the nth term of the sequence an by using the explicit fomula: $$a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d$$ Where $$n\geq2$$. Recursive formula Some arithmetic sequences are defined in terms of the previous term using a recursive formula: $$a_n = a_{n-1} + d$$ Where $$n\geq 2$$.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Sequences & Series > Sequences (A2 only)

resources.title: Arithmetic Series

content.topicNotes: Arithmetic Series An arithmetic series is the sum of the terms of an arithmetic sequence. Series The sum of the terms of a sequence is called a series. For the arithmetic sequence with $$a_1 = 5$$ and $$d = 2$$, the first four terms are: $$5,7,9,11$$ The series is then given by: $$5 +7+9+11 = 32$$ General formula We can write the sum of the first $$n$$ terms of an arithmetic series with a difference $$d$$ as: $$S_n = a_1 + (a_1+d)+ ...+(a_1+(n-2)d)+(a_1+(n-1)d)$$ Reversing the order of the terms, we can also write the sum as $$S_n = (a_1+(n-1)d)+(a_1+(n-2)d)+...+(a_1+d)+a_1$$ General formula Adding the two forms of $$S_n$$, we can see that the terms match up: $$2S_n = (2a_1+(n-1)d) + (2a_1+(n-1)d) +...+(2a_1+(n-1)d)+(2a_1+(n-1)d)$$ Because there are $$n$$ terms in the series, we can simplify this sum to: $$2S_n=n(2a_1+(n-1)d) \rightarrow S_n = \frac{1}{2}n(2a_1+(n-1)d)$$ Sum of natural numbers If we set $$a_1=1$$ and $$d=1$$, we can use the equation for the sum of an arithmetic series to find the sum of the first $$n$$ natural numbers: $$S_n = \frac{1}{2}n(2 + (n-1)) = \frac{\small n(n+1)}{\small 2}$$
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Sequences & Series > Sequences (A2 only)

resources.title: Binomial Expansion

content.topicNotes: Binomial Expansion We can work out the expansion of binomials using an equation involving factorials. Expanding binomials We have seen how we can expand binomials using the numbers in each row of Pascal's triangle. We've also seen how to work out the numbers in Pascal's triangle using factorials. This leads us to an equation we can use to expand binomials without having to think about Pascal's triangle. This is called the binomial expansion or binomial theorem. Binomial expansion equation The binomial expansion of $$(a+b)^n$$ is: $$(a+b)^n=a^n + {n\choose 1}a^{n-1}b + {n\choose 2}a^{n-2}b^2 + ...+{n \choose r}a^{n-r}b^{r}+...+ b^n$$ This equation applies when $$n \in$$ ℕ (is a positive whole number). This equation is included in the formula booklet in the exam. General term The general term in a binomial expansion is given by $${n \choose r}a^{n-r}b^{r}$$. We can use this to find coefficients of specific orders of variables in the binomial expansion. Example Use the binomial theorem to find the expansion of $$(1-6x)^5$$. Comparing variables If we compare the expression we want to expand with the equation given in the formula booklet: $$a = 1, b = -6x$$ and $$n = 5$$. So we can substitute these into each term to find the binomial expansion. First term The first term of the binomial expansion is $$a^n$$. Substituting in $$a = 1$$ and $$n = 5$$, we have: $$a^n = 1^5 = 1$$ Second term The second term of the binomial expansion is $${n\choose 1}a^{n-1}b$$. Substituting in for $$a,b$$ and $$n$$, we have: $${n\choose 1}a^{n-1}b = {5\choose 1}1^4(-6x)$$ Simplifying this term gives: $$\frac{5!}{1!\times4!}\times(-6x) = -30x$$ Third term The third term of the binomial expansion is $${n\choose 2}a^{n-2}b^2$$. Substituting in for $$a,b$$ and $$n$$, we have: $${n\choose 2}a^{n-2}b^2={5\choose 2}1^{3}(-6x)^2$$ Simplifying this term gives: $$\frac{5!}{2!\times3!}\times36x^2 = 10\times36x^2 = 360x^2$$ Fourth term The fourth term of the binomial expansion is $${n\choose 3}a^{n-3}b^3$$. Substituting in for $$a,b$$ and $$n$$, we have: $${n\choose 3}a^{n-3}b^3={5\choose 3}1^{2}(-6x)^3$$ Simplifying this term gives: $$\frac{5!}{3!\times2!}\times(-216)x^3 = 10\times(-216)x^3 = -2160x^3$$ Fifth term The fifth term of the binomial expansion is $${n\choose 4}a^{n-4}b^4$$. Substituting in for $$a,b$$ and $$n$$, we have: $${n\choose 4}a^{n-4}b^4 = {5\choose 4}ab^4$$ Simplifying this term gives: $$\frac{5!}{4!\times1!}\times1296x^4 = 5\times1296x^4 = 6480x^4$$ Final term The sixth term of the binomial expansion is $${n\choose 5}a^{n-5}b^5$$. We can tell that this is the final term in the expansion because there will be no powers of $$a$$ left in the term and that $${5\choose 5}=1$$. So this term is simply equal to $$b^n$$. Substituting in for $$b$$ and $$n$$, we have: $$b^n = (-6x)^5 = -7776x^5$$ Sum the terms The expansion of $$(1-6x)^5$$ is equal to the sum of the terms in the binomial expansion, so the answer is: $$(1-6x)^5 = 1 -30x + 360x^2 -2160x^3 + 6480x^4-7776x^5$$ Binomial Expansion The binomial expansion equation allows you to expand expressions of the form $$(a+b)^n$$ if $$n$$ is a positive whole number.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Sequences & Series > Binomial Expansion

resources.title: Binomial Expansion & Rational Powers (A2 only)

content.topicNotes: Binomial Expansion with Rational Powers If we have an expression $$(1+x)^n$$ and $$n$$ is a negative or rational number, we need to use a different equation for its expansion. Binomial expansion The binomial expansion of a the expression $$(1+x)^n$$ is equal to: $$1+ nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3 + ... + \frac{n(n-1)\times...\times(n-r+1)}{r!}x^r+...$$ This is an infinite sum of terms, also known as an infinite series. This expansion is valid when $$|x|<1$$ and $$n\in$$ ℝ (is a real number). This equation is included in the formula booklet in the exam. Binomial expansion We can use this equation to work out the expansion of binomials of the form $$(1+bx)^n$$ by grouping together $$(bx)$$ and treating it as if it was $$x$$: $$(1+bx)^n=1 + n(bx) + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}(bx)^2 + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}(bx)^3...$$ This expansion is valid when $$|bx|<1$$ or $$|x|<\frac{\small 1}{\small |b|}$$. Example What are the first four terms of the binomial expansion of $$(1+x)^{-2}$$? For which values of $$x$$ is the expansion valid? Comparing variables If we compare the expression we want to expand with the equation given in the formula booklet, we see that $$n = -2$$. So we can substitute this into each term to find the binomial expansion. First term The first term of this type of binomial expansion is always equal to 1. Second term The second term of the binomial expansion is $$nx$$. Substituting in $$n = -2$$, we get: $$nx = -2x$$ Third term The third term of the binomial expansion is $$\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2$$. Substituting in $$n = -2$$, we get: $$\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 = \frac{(-2)\times(-3)}{2\times1}x^2 = 3x^2$$ Fourth term The third term of the binomial expansion is $$\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3$$. Substituting in $$n = -2$$, we get: $$\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3=\frac{(-2)\times(-3)\times(-4)}{3\times2\times1}x^3 = -4x^3$$ Answer The first four terms of the binomial expansion of $$(1+x)^{-2}$$ are: $$(1+x)^{-2} = 1 -2x + 3x^2 - 4x^3 + ...$$ Validity The expansion is valid for values of $$x$$ such that $$|x|$$<1.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Sequences & Series > Binomial Expansion

resources.title: Binomial Expansion & Rational Powers 2 (A2 only)

content.topicNotes: Binomial Expansion for Rational Powers We can use the binomial expansion of $$(1+x)^n$$ to expand expressions of the form $$(a+bx)^n$$. Taking out factors In order to expand $$(a+bx)^n$$ using the binomial expansion, we need to take out a factor of $$a^n$$ and write it in front of the brackets: $$(a+bx)^n = ((a\times 1) + (a\times\frac{b}{a})x)^n = a^n\left(1+\frac{b}{a}x\right)^n$$ We can then expand $$(1+\frac{b}{a}x)^n$$ using the binomial expansion equation in the formula book, remembering to replace any $$x$$ terms with $$\frac{b}{a}x$$. Don't forget to multiply every term in the expansion by $$a^n$$ at the end to give the final answer. Example What are the first four terms of the binomial expansion of $$(3+2x)^{-2}$$? What are the range of values of $$x$$ for which the expansion is valid? Take out factors In order to use the expansion of $$(1+x)^n$$, we need to take out a factor of $$3^{-2}$$ from $$(3+2x)^{-2}$$" $$(3+2x)^{-2}=((3\times 1)+(3\times \frac{2}{3})x)^{-2} = 3^{-2}\left(1+\frac{2}{3}x\right)^{-2}$$ Expand $$(1+\frac{2}{3}x)^{-2}$$ The first term of the expansion of $$\left(1+\frac{2}{3}x\right)^{-2}$$ is equal to 1. Second term The second term of the binomial expansion of is $$nx$$. Substituting in $$n = -2$$ and noticing that we must change $$x \rightarrow \frac{2}{3}x$$, we get $$nx \rightarrow -\frac{4}{3}x$$ Third term The third term of the binomial expansion is $$\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2$$. Substituting in $$n = -2$$ and changing $$x \rightarrow \frac{2}{3}x$$, we get: $$\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 \rightarrow \frac{(-2)\times(-3)}{2\times1}\left(\frac{2}{3}x\right)^2 = \frac{4}{3}x^2$$ Fourth term The third term of the binomial expansion is $$\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3$$. Substituting in $$n = -2$$ and changing $$x \rightarrow \frac{2}{3}x$$, we get: $$\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3 \rightarrow \frac{(-2)\times(-3)\times(-4)}{3\times2\times1}\left(\frac{2}{3}x\right)^3 = -\frac{32}{27}x^3$$ Add terms The expansion of $$(1+\frac{2}{3}x)^{-2}$$ is equal to: $$\left(1+\frac{2}{3}x\right)^{-2}=1-\frac{4}{3}x+\frac{4}{3}x^2 -\frac{32}{27}x^3+...$$ Multiply each term by $$3^{-2}$$ To find the final answer, we need to multiply the whole expansion by $$3^{-2}=\frac{1}{9}$$: $$(3+2x)^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}=\frac{4}{27}x+\frac{4}{27}x^2-\frac{32}{243}x^3+...$$ Validity The binomial expansion is valid when $$\left|\frac{2}{3}x\right|<1$$, which means: $$\left|x\right|<1.5$$

resources.title: Circle Theorems - Angle at a Semi-Circle

content.topicNotes: Circle Theorems Angle in a semicircle is 90° Proof Split the triangle into two triangles which are both isosceles since they both have two sides which are radii. Mark one of the angles at the centre x. Proof continued y = 1⁄2(180° - x) since the triangle is isosceles and all angles add up to 180°. Similarly z = 1⁄2(180° - (180° - x)) = 1⁄2x Therefore the angle at the circumference is z + y = 1⁄2 × 180° = 90° as required. Alternative proof Alternatively, using the previous theorem we see that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference. So 180° is twice the angle at the circumference so the angle is 90°.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Coordinate Geometry > Circles

resources.title: Circle Theorems - Angle at the Centre

content.topicNotes: Circle Theorems Angle at centre is double the angle at the circumference Proof Split the shape into two isosceles triangles and label the angles. The angle at the centre is 360° - x - y and the angle at the circumference is a + b. Proof continued Since the angles in a triangle add up to 180°: a = 1⁄2(180° - y), b = 1⁄2(180° - x) So angle at circumference = a + b = 1⁄2(360° - x - y) = 1⁄2 × angle at centre.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Coordinate Geometry > Circles

resources.title: Circle Theorems - Perpendicular Bisector

content.topicNotes: Circle Theorems Perpendicular bisector goes through centre The perpendicular bisector of a chord always goes through the centre of the circle. Proof Draw the perpendicular from centre, O, to the chord AB. Draw a radius to A and another to B to form two triangles. Proof continued Their hypotenuses are the same length (because they are both radii) and they share another edge so the triangles are congruent by the ‘RHS’ rule. Therefore AM = BM and so the perpendicular splits the chord exactly in half.

resources.title: Circumcircle of a Right-angled Triangle

content.topicNotes: Circumcircle of a Right-Angled Triangle The circumcircle of a right-angled triangle is easily found by looking at the midpoint of its hypotenuse. Triangle in a semi-circle There is a circle theorem that states that the angle of a triangle at the circumference of a semi-circle is always 90°. This means that the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is the diameter of its circumcircle. We can use this to find the equation of the circumcircle of the triangle. How do you find the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle? To identify which two vertices of the triangle form the hypotenuse, we first need to find the square of the length of each side. We can identify the hypotenuse using Pythagoras' theorem: Opposite side2 + adjacent side2 = hypotenuse2 How do you find the equation of the circumcircle? To write the general equation of the circumcircle, we need to find the centre and the radius of the circle. The centre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse. The radius is half the length of the hypotenuse. Example The points A(3,6), B(3,4) and C(4,5) lie on the circumference of a circle. Show that ABC is a right-angled triangle. Find the equation of the circle. Work out the length of each side squared $$AB^2 = 2^2 = 4$$ $$AC^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2$$ $$BC^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2$$ Use Pythagoras' theorem All right-angled triangles satisfy Pythagoras' theorem. We can see that $$AC^2 + BC^2=AB^2 $$ as 2 + 2 = 4. This means that $$ABC$$ is a right-angled triangle with $$AB$$ as its hypotenuse. Use circle theorem $$ABC$$ is a right-angled triangle, so $$AB$$ is the diameter of its circumcircle. Find the centre The centre of the circumcircle is the midpoint of the diameter $$AB$$. Midpoint = $$(\frac{3+3}{2},\frac{6+4}{2}) = (3,5)$$ Find the radius As calculated earlier, $$AB^2$$ = 4. This means: Diameter $$AB$$ = 2 Radius = 1 Write the equation of the circle We can now write the equation of the circumcircle in its general form: $$(x-3)^2 + (y-5)^2 = 1$$

resources.title: Compound Growth & Decay

content.topicNotes: Compound Growth and Decay Growth and decay When an amount increases or decreases by a set percentage on a regular basis this is called compound growth or compound decay. The amount that is lost/gained changes with each interval since the amount lost/gained is a percentage of the current amount. Formula This formula gives the amount after n intervals: N = S × (multiplier)n Where S is the starting amount and the multiplier is the percentage multiplier: 1.25 for a 25% increase or 0.6 for a 40% decrease.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Exponentials & Logarithms > Exponential Growth  Decay

resources.title: Compund Interest

content.topicNotes: Compound Interest In summer, the number of ants in a colony increases by 20% each day. On the first day there are 10,000 ants. How many days until the colony numbers more than 30,000? The formula for compound interest N is the number of ants n is the number of days passed On the 5th day there are 24 883 ants (to nearest whole number) On the 6th day there are 28 860 ants On the 7th day there are 35 832 ants Answer This is the first day we are over 30 000 so the answer is 7 days. Number of ants per hour By using the rule for raising a power to another power, we can convert the multiplier for the growth after $$n$$ days into one that shows the growth every hour This way we see that there is a 0.8% increase in the number of ants every hour.

resources.title: Depreciation

content.topicNotes: Depreciation Depreciation can be thought of as when something gets reduces over time. This might be the value of a car or the volume of water in a bath. Linear decay Linear decay is when something decreases by a steady amount over set time periods. E.g. pulling the plug out of a bath will reduce the volume of water in the bath by a set amount each second. Exponential decay Exponential decay is when something decreases by a multiplier (or percentage) over set time periods. Exponential decay example A car costs $10,000 when it's new. The value of a car reduces by 10% every two months. After two months, its value has decreased by 10%. It is now worth $10,000 × 0.9 = $9,000. After another two months, it is worth $9,000 × 0.9 = $8,100. After another two months, it is worth $8,100 × 0.9 = $7,290. After another two months, it is worth $7,290 × 0.9 = $6,561.

content.topicNotes: Derivatives The derivative of a function, f(x), is the function that describes how the gradient changes as x changes. This is the same as saying that the derivative is the rate of change of an equation. Derivatives The derivative of a function can be used to calculate the gradient of the function at any point. The derivative of f($$x$$) is called f'($$x$$). f'($$x$$) can be called "f dash of $$x$$" or "f prime". Example A function, f($$x$$), has the derivative, f'($$x$$) = 2$$x$$ + 5 What is the gradient of f($$x$$) when $$x$$ = 3? Gradient at $$x$$ = 3 is f'(3). f'(3) = (2 × 3) + 5 = 11 f($$x$$) has a gradient of 11 when $$x$$ = 3. Derivatives The derivative of a function, f(x), is a function, f'(x), the describes how the slope of a graph changes how x changes. Tangents The derivative tells you the gradient of a tangent to a graph at any value of x.

resources.title: Differentiation from First Principles - Practice

content.topicNotes: What is Differentiation by First Principles? Differentiation by first principles is a method used to find the general expression for the derivate of a function. What is the derivative of a function? The derivative of $$f(x)$$ is an expression that tells us exactly what the gradient of a given function is for any value of $$x$$. What is the equation for the derivative? The derivative of a function is given by the equation: $$f\prime(x)= \lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$ How do we find the gradient using the derivative? To find the gradient of a function at a point $$(x,f(x))$$ we need to work out the values of $$f(x+h)$$ and $$f(x)$$. We can then substitute this into the derivative equation. Finally, we work out what the expression is equal to when $$h$$ tends to 0. This gives the gradient at that point. How do we find the limit as $$h\to0$$? As you take the limit as $$h$$ tends to zero, any constant terms that do not contain a factor of $$h$$ will stay the same: For example, $$\lim\limits_{h\to0}5=5$$ Any terms that contain at least one factor of $$h$$ will tend to zero as $$h$$ tends to zero: For example, $$\lim\limits_{h\to0}3h=\lim\limits_{h\to0}h^2=\lim\limits_{h\to0}2h^8=0$$

content.topicNotes: Direct Proportion Two variables are directly proportional to one another if the size of one variable increases when the size of other increases. Directly proportional If $$x$$ and $$y$$ are directly proportional to one another, we write: $$x\large{\propto} y$$ Where $$\large \propto$$ is the symbol of proportionality. We can always write the equation: $$x = ky$$ Where $$k$$ is called the constant of proportionality and is a non-zero number. Proportional For example, the area of a square is proportional to the length of one side squared, so we can write $$A\large{\propto} x^2 \rightarrow A=x^2$$ In this case, the constant of proportionality $$k$$ is equal to 1.

resources.title: Double Angle Formula

content.topicNotes: Double Angle Formulae The double angle formulae are special cases of the angle addition formulae where $$A = B$$. Sine The double angle formula for sine is: $$\sin2A \equiv \sin A\cos A + \cos A\sin A\equiv 2\sin A\cos A$$ Cosine The double angle formula for cosine is: $$\cos2A \equiv \cos A\cos A - \sin A\sin A\equiv \cos^2A - \sin^2A$$ Cosine cont. We can find equivalent identities by using the fact that $$\cos^2A + \sin^2A = 1$$: $$\cos2A\equiv 1-2\sin^2A\equiv 2\cos^2A-1$$ Tangent The double angle formula for tangent is: $$\tan2A\equiv \frac{\tan A+\tan A}{1 - \tan A \tan A}\equiv\frac{2\tan A}{1-\tan^2 A}$$

resources.title: Equation of a Circumcircle

content.topicNotes: Equation of a Circumcircle of a Triangle from Three Points We can find the general equation of a circumcircle of a triangle by using the properties of chords. What is a circumcircle? The circumcircle of a triangle is the circumference of a circle upon which the three vertices of the triangle lie. A group of three points can only have one circumcircle. What is a circumcircle? Each side of the triangle is a chord of the circle. The perpendicular bisectors of the triangle sides intersect at the centre of the circle. How do you find the equation of a circumcircle? To write the general equation of the circumcircle, we need to find the centre and the radius of the circle. How do you find the equation of a circumcircle? The centre is found by working out the point of intersection between the perpendicular bisectors of two of the sides of the triangle. The radius is found by working out the distance between the centre of the circle and one of the points of the triangle. Example The points A(-6,3), B(-3,2) and C(0,3) lie on the circumference of a circle. What is the equation of the circle? Find the perpendicular bisector of AB The gradient of the chord AB is equal to: $$ \frac{2-3}{(-3) - (-6)}=-\frac{1}{3}$$ The gradient of the perpendicular bisector of AB must be equal to 3. The midpoint of AB has coordinates: Midpoint = $$(\frac{(-6)+(-3)}{2},\frac{3+2}{2}) = (-4.5,2.5)$$ Find the perpendicular bisector of AB The intercept of the perpendicular bisector, $$c$$ is then found from: $$y = 3x + c$$ Find the perpendicular bisector of AB Substituting in the midpoint coordinates, we get: $$2.5 = (3 \times (-4.5)) + c$$ $$2.5 = -13.5 +c \rightarrow c = 16$$ So the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB is $$y = 3x +16$$ Find the perpendicular bisector of AC The gradient of the chord AC is equal to: $$ \frac{3-3}{0 - (-6)}=0$$ This means that AC is horizontal. The equation for the perpendicular bisector must be: $$x = \frac{(-6)+0}{2} = -3$$ Find the centre of the circumcircle The centre of the circumcircle is the point of intersection between the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC. Find the centre of the circumcircle Substituting in $$x=3$$ into $$y = 3x +16$$, we get: $$y = (3 \times 3) +16 \rightarrow y = 7$$ The centre of the circumcircle has coordinates (3,7). Find the radius of the circumcircle The radius of the circumcircle is equal to the distance between the centre and any one of the points of the triangle. Find the radius of the circumcircle The distance between the centre and point $$A$$ is found by using Pythagoras' theorem: Distance $$= \sqrt{(3-(-6))^2 + (7-3)^2} = 5$$ The radius of the circumcircle is equal to 5. Write the equation of the circumcircle We can now write the equation of the circumcircle in its general form: $$(x+3)^2 + (y-7)^2 = 25$$

resources.title: Equation of a Perpendicular Bisector

content.topicNotes: Perpendicular Bisector of a Chord We can find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of a chord using the properties of straight lines graphs. What is the perpendicular bisector of a chord? The perpendicular bisector of a chord is the perpendicular line that passes through the midpoint of the chord. The perpendicular bisector of a chord always passes through the centre of the circle. What is the gradient of the perpendicular bisector? We first need to find the gradient of the chord using the equation: $$m_c = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$$ Where $$(x_1,y_1)$$ and $$(x_2,y_2)$$ are the points where the chord meets the circumference. The bisector is perpendicular to the chord, so its gradient $$m_b$$ satisfies: $$m_b\times m_c=-1$$ What is the gradient of the perpendicular bisector? What is the equation of the perpendicular bisector? We can then find the equation of the bisector by working out the midpoint of the chord: Midpoint = $$(\frac{\small x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{\small y_1+y_2}{2})$$ Finally, we substitute this into the general equation of a straight line with gradient $$m_b$$ to find the $$y$$-intercept $$c$$: $$y = m_bx + c$$ Example The points $$A(3,7)$$ and $$B(6,4)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle. What is the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the chord AB? Find the gradient of chord The gradient of the chord is given by: $$m_c = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}=\frac{4-7}{6-3}=-\frac{3}{3}=-1$$ Find the gradient of bisector The gradient of the perpendicular bisector $$m_b$$ satisfies the equation: $$m_b\times m_c = -1$$ $$m_b = -\frac{1}{m_c} = 1$$ Find the midpoint of chord The midpoint of the chord AB is equal to: midpoint = $$(\frac{\small x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{\small y_1+y_2}{2}) = (\frac{3+6}{2},\frac{7+4}{2}) = (4.5, 5.5)$$ Find the y-intercept of the perpendicular bisector Substitute $$m_b$$ and the midpoint into the general equation of a straight line: $$y = m_bx+c$$ $$5.5 = 1\times 4.5 + c$$ Rearranging for $$c$$, we get: $$c = 5.5 - 4.5 =1$$ Final answer So the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the chord AB is: $$y =x + 1$$ Perpendicular Bisector of a Chord The perpendicular bisector of a chord is the line that exactly halves the chord at an angle of 90°. That means their point of intersection is at the midpoint of the chord.

resources.title: Exponential Function

content.topicNotes: Exponential Functions Functions that are linear show growth or decay that occurs at a steady rate. The exponential function models growth or decay with an increasing rate. Definition For any real number $$x$$, an exponential function is a function with the form" $$f(x) = ab^x$$ Where $$a$$ is a non-zero real number called the initial value and $$b$$ is any positive real number such that $$b\ne1$$. We call $$b$$ the base of the exponential function. $$f(x) = 3^x$$ has base 3. Exponential growth Exponential growth means that the original value increases by the same percentage over equal increments found in the domain. As the value grows, so does the percentage of the value. Linear growth means the original value increases by the same amount over equal increments found in the domain. Exponential growth The table shows the values for which the exponential function of base 2 is larger than linear and quadratic functions. In general, the exponential function will always eventually outgrow any polynomial. Graph The $$y$$-intercept of an exponential function is $$(0,a)$$. For a function with no initial value such as $$f(x)=2^x$$, this intercept is always equal to 1. The graph does not cross the $$x$$-axis, instead getting closer toward it for very large and negative values of $$x$$. Properties The domain of $$f(x) = ab^x$$ is all of the real numbers. The range is all positive real numbers if $$a>0$$. The range is all negative real numbers if $$a<0$$.

resources.title: Factorials

content.topicNotes: Factorial Notation Factorial notation is used as shorthand for certain products of numbers. Factorials The factorial of a number is equal to the number multiplied by all of the natural numbers smaller than it: For example, 4 factorial is equal to 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. Factorial notation Factorial notation makes writing factorials easier. The factorial of a whole number $$n$$ is written as $$n!$$. 6 factorial = $$6! = 6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1 = 720$$ Factorials The factorial of 0 is defined to be equal to 1. Applications Factorials are used in many areas of maths. One common use of factorials is counting the number of ways to pick or arrange objects. For example, if you have 3 unique items, the number of ways to arrange these items is equal to $$3!=3\times2\times1=6$$. Applications We can use factorials to work out the number of ways to pick $$r$$ distinct objects from a collection of $$n$$ objects. This number is called "$$n$$ choose $$r$$" and is written as $$^{n}C_{r}$$ or $$n\choose r$$: $${n\choose r} = \frac{\small n!}{\small r!(n-r)!}$$ Example A restaurant offers five side dish options. Your meal comes with two side dishes. How many ways can you select your side dishes? The total number of options $$n=5$$, and $$r=2$$, so we work out $$5\choose 2$$: $${5\choose 2} = \frac{\small 5!}{\small 2!(5-3)!}= \frac{\small 5!}{\small 2!3!} = \frac{\small 120}{\small 2\times6} = 10$$ Connection to Pascal's triangle We can work out each number in each row of Pascal's triangle using $$n\choose r$$. The $$r$$th number in the $$n$$th row of Pascal's triangle is equal to: $$^{n-1}C_{r-1}={n-1\choose r-1} = \frac{(n-1)!}{(r-1)!((n-1)-(r-1))!}=\frac{(n-1)!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}$$ Example The 3rd number of the 4th row in Pascal's triangle is equal to: $$^{3}C_{2}={3\choose2} = \frac{3!}{2!1!} = \frac{6}{2} = 3$$

resources.title: Factorise Quadratics

content.topicNotes: Factorising Quadratics We can solve quadratics using factorisation. We get two solutions, one from each bracket. Find pairs of numbers which multiply to give (-8) Choose the pair which also adds to give 2 These numbers multiply to give (-8) and add to give 2 Write these two numbers in the brackets We have now factorised the equation One solution is when the first bracket = 0 This gives x = 2 The second solution is when the second bracket = 0 This gives x = -4 These are the two solutions to the quadratic Factorising Quadratics Follow these steps to factorise an expression of the form ax² + bx + c where a is not 1. We use 2x² + 10x + 8 as an example. Step 1 Work out the initial set of brackets. The coefficients of x must multiply to give a (a = 2 in this example). Step 2 Find pairs of numbers that multiply to give c (8 in this case). Step 3 Trial and error until you find a combination that works. Try each pair both ways round (e.g. 2 in the 2x bracket or in the x bracket) and with different signs until you find a combination that results in the correct x coefficient in the expansion. Step 4 Always expand to check your answer works.

content.topicNotes: Differentiation The derivative of a function can be worked out through a process called differentiation. Differentiation There are different ways to display the derivative of a function. If your equation starts with y =, then the derivative of the equation is $$\large\frac{dy}{dx}$$. If your function starts with f($$x$$) =, then the derivative of the equation is f'($$x$$). The exam may also ask you to find the rate of change, the gradient of the tangent or to differentiate a function. General rule To differentiate a whole equation/function, each term should be differentiated individually. The general rule for differentiating a term is: f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 Examples f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 f($$x$$) = $$x$$3 → f'($$x$$) = 3$$x$$2 f($$x$$) = 2$$x$$3 → f'($$x$$) = 6$$x$$2 f($$x$$) = 6$$x$$ → f'($$x$$) = 6 (remember f($$x$$) = 6$$x$$ is the same as 6$$x$$1) f($$x$$) = 3$$x$$4 → f'($$x$$) = 12$$x$$3 f($$x$$) = 9 → f'($$x$$) = 0 (remember f($$x$$) = 9 is the same as 9$$x$$0) Example 1 with multiple terms For each term in an expression, use f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 f($$x$$) = $$x$$3 + 2$$x$$2 + 7$$x$$ f'($$x$$) = 3$$x$$2 + 4$$x$$ + 7 Example 1 with multiple terms For each term in an expression, use f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 f($$x$$) = 3$$x$$4 + 5$$x$$3 + 4$$x$$2 f'($$x$$) = 12$$x$$3 + 15$$x$$2 + 8$$x$$

resources.title: Finding the Centre & Radius

content.topicNotes: How do you find the Centre and Radius of a Circle? To find the centre and radius of a circle from its expanded equation, we need to complete the square. What is the expanded equation of a circle? If we expand the general equation of a circle with centre $$(a,b)$$ and radius $$r$$ we get: $$(x - a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2$$ $$x^2 -2ax + a^2 +y^2 -2by +b^2=r^2 $$ $$x^2 +y^2 -2ax -2by +a^2+b^2-r^2 = 0$$ What is the expanded equation of a circle? If we make the substitutions: $$a = -f$$ $$b = -g$$ $$a^2+b^2-r^2= c$$ Then the expanded form of the equation of a circle is given by: $$x^2+y^2 +2fx +2gy+c = 0$$ How do you find the centre and radius of a circle? If the equation of a circle is in the expanded form, we can complete the square and find the circle in the general form: $$(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 = r^2$$. The centre of the circle is at the point $$(a,b)$$ and the radius is of length $$r$$. Example What is the centre and radius of the circle with equation $$x^2 + y^2-4x-6y+4 = 0$$? Group together $$x$$ and $$y$$ terms To begin, we group together the terms containing $$x$$ and the terms containing $$y$$: $$x^2 -4x + y^2 - 6y + 4 = 0$$ Complete the square for terms containing $$x$$ We then complete the square for the $$x$$ terms alone: $$x^2 -4x = (x-2)^2 -4$$ Complete the square for terms containing $$7$$ We then complete the square for the $$y$$ terms alone: $$y^2 -6y = (y-3)^2 -9$$ Substitute in We then substitute these back into the equation: $$(x-2)^2 - 4 + (y-3)^2 -9 +4=0$$ Simplify Simplifying the constants gives: $$(x-2)^2 + (y-3)^2 -9 = 0$$ Then adding 9 (which is 32) to each side, we get the equation of the circle in its general form: $$(x-2)^2 + (y-3)^2 = 3^2$$ Inspect Comparing this to the general form of the equation, we can see that the centre of the circle is at the point (2,3) and the radius is equal to 3.

resources.title: Geometric Sequences

content.topicNotes: Geometric Sequences A geometric sequence is one in which any term divided by the previous term is a constant. Common ratio This constant is called the common ratio of the sequence. The common ratio can be found by dividing any term in the sequence by the previous term. Explicit formula If $$a_1$$ is the initial term of a geometric sequence and $$r$$ is the common ratio, the explicit equation to find a particular term $$a_n$$ is: $$a_n = a_1r^{n-1}$$ Recursive formula A recursive formula allows us to find any term of a geometric sequence by using the previous term: $$a_n=ra_{n-1}$$ For $$n\geq 2$$

resources.title: Geometric Series

content.topicNotes: Geometric Series The sum of the terms in a geometric sequence is called a geometric series. Series The sum of the terms of a sequence is called a series. For the geometric sequence defined by $$a_n = 5\times 2^n$$, the first four terms are: $$5,10,20,40$$ The series is then given by: $$5 +10+20+40$$ The sum of this series is 75. General formula We can write the sum of the first $$n$$ terms of a geometric series with common ratio $$r$$ as: $$S_n = a_1 + ra_1+ ...+ r^{n-1}a_1$$ Multiplying both sides of the equation by $$r$$ we have: $$rS_n = ra_1 + r^2a_1+...+ r^na_1$$ General formula Subtracting this from the original equation for $$S_n$$, almost all of the terms cancel out: $$S_n - rS_n = a_1 - r^na_1$$ Taking out a factor of $$S_n$$ and dividing by $$1-r$$, we have the general equation for the sum of a geometric series: $$\large S_n = \large a_1 \frac{\large(1-r^n)}{\large(1-r)},; r\ne 1$$

content.topicNotes: Gradient and y-intercept of a Line A line y = mx + c has gradient m and y-intercept c. y-intercept The point where a line crosses the y-axis is called the y-intercept. Gradient To calculate the gradient (slope) of a line, use 2 co-ordinates (A and B): gradient = change in y ÷ change in x where change in y = (yA - yB) and change in x = (xA - xB) Finding the Equation of a Line From a Graph We can calculate the equation of a line if we have two points on the line or one point and the gradient. Given two points - method To find the equation of a line between two points, first calculate the gradient m. Then substitute in one of the points into the equation and rearrange to find c. For example to find the equation of the line between (2,4) and (-1,2)... Given two points - step 1 Find the gradient: change in y = 4 - 2 = 2 change in x = 2 - (-1) = 3 so m = 2⁄3 Given two points - step 2 We know the line is y = 2⁄3x + c so substitute in x = 2 and y = 4 to find c: (4) = 2⁄3(2) + c so c = 8⁄3 Therefore the line is y = 2⁄3x + 8⁄3. Given gradient and point To find the equation of a line with a given gradient and going through a point substitute in the point to the line y = mx + c where m is the gradient you’ve been given.

Cube root graph The cube root of a negative number gives a negative number, so the graph exists in both quadrants I and III. Absolute value function The absolute value function is written as $$f(x) = |x|$$. The function takes each value of $$x$$ and gives the magnitude of the value as its output. For example, $$f(-9) = \left|-9\right| = 9$$ The graph exists only in the upper two quadrants of the Cartesian plane. Piecewise function A piecewise function is a function that is composed of multiple functions defined on different ranges of $$x$$. The convention for writing the function is shown alongside the graph. Step function The step function is a special type of piecewise function. The step function is 0 for negative values of $$x$$ and 1 for positive values of $$x$$ and for $$x=0$$.

content.topicNotes: Direct and Inverse Proportion Graphs We can show the two different types of proportionality between two variables on a graph. Direct proportion If y and x are directly proportional, the graph of the relationship will be a straight line graph. It must pass through the origin. It could have a negative slope. y = 2x For every increase in x, y increases by twice that amount. Since it goes through the origin, y is always double x. y is directly proportional to x with k = 2. y = 2x + 3 This graph shows y = 2x + 3. Every increase in x corresponds to twice that increase in y. y is not directly proportional to x because of the '+ 3'. Inverse proportion If y and x are inversely proportional then the graph is a curved line that never touches the x or y axes. Part of the graph lies in quadrant I and part of the graph lies in quadrant III. Unit rate The constant of proportionality can also be thought of as a unit rate, or "y per unit x". The unit rate is equal to the y-coordinate of the graph when x = 1.

resources.title: Integration - Basics

content.topicNotes: Integration Integration is the opposite of differentiation. Integration To integrate $$x^n$$, add one to the power of x and divide by the new power. $$x^n \rightarrow \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$$ Terms with no powers of $$x$$ differentiate to nothing. So we must add an extra unknown "constant of integration" after we integrate: $$x^n \rightarrow \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c$$ This rule only works for $$n \ne 1$$. Example If $$y = x^3 - 5$$, then $$\frac{dy}{dx}= 3x^2$$. If $$y = x^3 +100$$, then $$\frac{dy}{dx}= 3x^2$$. So if we integrate $$\frac{dy}{dx}= 3x^2$$, we have to add the extra term: $$\frac{dy}{dx}= 3x^2 \rightarrow y = x^3 + c$$ Constant of integration To find the constant of integration, we need to know a value of $$y$$ for a specific value of $$x$$. Substitute these values into the equation after integrating and rearrange for $$c$$. Example What is the equation of the curve that has gradient $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2 + 2$$ and passes through the point $$(3,12)$$? The gradient of a curve is equal to the differential of the equation of the curve, so we must integrate the gradient to get the equation of the curve. $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2 + 2 \rightarrow y=\frac{x^3}{3} + 2x + c$$ Example To find $$c$$, substitute $$x = 3$$ and $$y = 12$$: $$12 = \frac{3^3}{3} + 6 + c$$ $$c = -3$$ So the equation of the curve is $$y = \frac{x^3}{3} + 2x-3$$

resources.title: Integration by Parts - Practice

content.topicNotes: What is Integration by Parts? Integration by parts is a method used to integrate the product of two functions. It uses the product rule of differentiation to form an equation that lets us rewrite the integral in a simpler way. Integration by parts The equation for integration by parts is: $$\int u\frac{dv}{dx}dx = uv-\int v\frac{du}{dx}dx$$ This equation is included in the formula booklet, although it is not named, so you'll need to remember which one it is! Choosing functions In order to use the integration by parts equation, we need to choose which function is $$u$$ and which function is $$\frac{dv}{dx}$$. The combination you choose should make the integral $$\int v \frac{du}{dx}dx$$ simpler than the original integral you need to solve. Constant of integration The constant of integration is only included at the very end of the calculation.

Estimating values You can use a graph to estimate values. The graph shows the value of a car over an 8 year period. Estimate how much the car is worth after 2 years and after 6 years. Example After 2 years the car is worth approximately $4,900. After 6 years the car is worth approximately $1,200. Finding the multiplier You can also use a graph to find out the rate of growth/decay. After 3 years the value is approximately $3,450. After 4 years the value is approximately $2,400. Multiplier example cont. resources.title: Logarithms

content.topicNotes: Logarithms In order to solve equations with exponential functions in them, we need to define the inverse of the exponential operation. Logarithm The logarithmic function is written as $$\log_b(x)=y$$, which is equivalent to $$x=b^y$$. $$b$$ is called the base of the logarithm. To remember this, think "left to the right equals middle". The base 2 logarithm of the number 8 is 3, so $$\log_2(8)=3\Leftrightarrow2^3=8$$ Range and domain The range of the exponential function is the set of positive real numbers. This means the domain of a logarithm is the set of positive real numbers. So we can only define $$\log_b$$ for $$x>0$$. We also specified that the allowed range of values of the base $$b$$ of the exponential function was the positive real numbers excluding the number 1. So we can only define $$\log_bx$$ for $$b>0,b\ne1$$. Properties For single variables and numbers, we often drop the parenthesis to make logarithms easy to write. The logarithm of the number one is equal to zero for any base, so: $$\log_b1=0$$ For logarithms of base 10, we often drop the base number and write: $$\log_{10}x=\log x$$ Graph The graph of $$y=\log_bx$$ does not cross the $$y$$-axis. The $$x-$$-intercept is 1. The orientation of the graph is different for values of $$b>0$$ and $$0<b<1$$ as shown. Logarithms To convert between exponential and logarithmic expressions, remember "left to the right equals middle".

resources.title: Manipulating the Angle Addition Formulae

content.topicNotes: Manipulating the Angle Addition Formulae We can prove other angle addition formulae by manipulating what we have already for $$\sin(A+B)$$ and $$\cos(A+B)$$. Sine subtraction formula We can find the identity for $$\sin(A-B)$$ by substituting $$B \rightarrow-B$$ into the identity for $$\sin(A+B)$$: $$\sin(A+(-B)) \equiv \sin A\cos(- B) + \cos A\sin (-B)$$ $$\sin(A-B) \equiv \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B$$ Where we have used $$\cos(-B) = \cos B$$ and $$\sin(-B) = -\sin B$$. Cosine subtraction formula We can find the identity for $$\cos(A-B)$$ by substituting $$B \rightarrow-B$$ into the identity for $$\cos(A+B)$$: $$\cos(A+(-B)) \equiv \cos A\cos(- B) - \sin A\sin (-B)$$ $$\cos(A-B) \equiv \cos A\cos B +\sin A\sin B$$ Where we have used $$\cos(-B) = \cos B$$ and $$\sin(-B) = -\sin B$$. Tangent addition formula To find the addition formula for tangent, we $$\tan(A+B) \equiv \frac{\sin(A+B)}{\cos(A+B)}$$ Substituting in our angle addition formulas, we get: $$\tan(A+B) \equiv \frac{\sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B -\sin A\sin B}$$ Dividing both the numerator and denominator by a factor of $$\cos A\cos B$$ gives: $$\tan(A+B) \equiv \frac{\small \frac{\sin A\cos B}{\cos A\cos B} + \frac{\cos A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B}}{\small \frac{\cos A\cos B}{\cos A\cos B} - \frac{\sin A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B}}$$ Tangent addition formula cont. Cancelling out common factors gives: $$\tan(A+B) \equiv \frac{\small \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \frac{\sin B}{\cos B}}{\small 1 - \frac{\sin A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B}}$$ Finally, we can simplify this as: $$\tan(A+B)\equiv \frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1 - \tan A \tan B}$$ Negative tangent We can find the identity for $$\tan(A-B)$$ by substituting $$B \rightarrow-B$$ into the identity for $$\tan(A+B)$$: $$\tan(A+(-B))\equiv \frac{\tan A+\tan (-B)}{1 - \tan A \tan(- B)}$$ $$\tan(A-B) \equiv \frac{\tan A-\tan B}{1 + \tan A\tan B}$$ Where we have used $$\tan(-B) = -\tan B$$.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Trigonometry > Trigonometric Identities

resources.title: Mathematical Proof

content.topicNotes: What is Mathematical Proof? A proof is a mathematical argument that explicitly shows that a given statement is always true. What is the difference between a theorem and a conjecture? A theorem is a mathematical statement that has been proven to always be true. A conjecture is a mathematical statement that has not been proven to always be true yet. You will be asked to prove that a given conjecture is true. What are assumptions in proofs? Assumptions are the conditions under which the conjecture is true. For example, a common assumption is that a conjecture holds for all positive integers. If we know a number is a positive integer, then its square must also be a positive integer. We can then use this fact as a step in a proof. How do you write numbers in proofs? If we know that a number is even, we can rewrite it as $$2n$$, where $$n$$ is an integer. If we know that a number is odd, we can rewrite it as $$2n+1$$, where $$n$$ is an integer. Consecutive numbers are written as $$n, n+1,n+2,...$$ Mathematical Proof All theorems in maths need to go through a process of being shown to be true in all cases. This process is called mathematical proof.
content.description: Maths: Edexcel A Level Pure Maths > Proof > Proof

resources.title: Maxima & Minima

content.topicNotes: Maxima & Minima Calculus can be used to find the maximum and minimum values of physical quantities. Turnings points The turning point of a graph is any coordinate on a graph where the gradient = 0. Different types of turning points include: Maxima, where the function is largest. Minima, where the function is the smallest. Turning points The gradient of a graph is equal to the derivative of the graph. -The $$x$$-coordinate of a turning point is found by setting $$f\prime(x)$$ or $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ equal to zero. It is called a turning point because the graph often changes direction at f'($$x$$) = 0. Kinematics We can use the same method to work out the maximum and minimum values of physical quantities if they are expressed as a function of time. For example, if $$v = -2t^2+t+4$$: $$\frac{dv}{dt} = -4t + 1 = 0 \rightarrow t = 0.25$$ s. $$v = -2\times0.25^2 + 0.25 + 4 = 4.38$$ m/s (2 d.p.). So there is a turning point at $$v = 4.38$$ m/s, which is the maximum value due to the shape of the graph.

resources.title: Modelling with Parametric Equations

content.topicNotes: Modelling with Parametric Equations Parametric equations are used to model real-life situations. Models A mathematical model is a set of equations that describe a real-life situation or object. Answering a question about a model that uses parametric equations will require you to give your answer in units that are relevant to the question. You may also have to comment on how realistic a model is in the context of the question. Time We can define a set of parametric equations with time as the parameter. Then $$x$$ and $$y$$ are defined as functions of time that describe the two-dimensional motion of an object. Example A remote-controlled boat is driven on the surface of a lake. The position (in metres) of the boat at time $$t$$ seconds is modelled by the parametric equations: $$x = 5t,;;;y=15t,;;;t>0$$ Show that the motion of the remote-controlled boat is a straight line. Find the speed of the remote-controlled boat. Rearrange $$x$$ equation To find the Cartesian equation, rearrange the equation for $$x$$ to get $$t$$ on its own: $$x = 5t \rightarrow t = \frac{x}{5}$$ Find the Cartesian equation Substitute this into the equation for $$y$$ gives: $$y = 15 \div \frac{x}{5} = 3x$$ Inspection The equation $$y = 3x$$ is a straight line with gradient 3 and a $$y$$-intercept of 0. $$x$$ and $$y$$ are the position of the boat, so the boat is moving in a straight line. Find the speed of the boat Remember the equation for speed: Speed = $$\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$$ Find the speed in each direction In the $$x$$-direction, the speed is: Speed = $$\frac{5t}{t} = 5$$ m/s In the $$y$$-direction, the speed is: Speed = $$ \frac{15t}{t} = 15$$ m/s Find the magnitude of the speed The overall size of the speed of the boat is given by Pythagoras' theorem: Speed = $$\sqrt{(5)^2+(15)^2} = 15.81$$ m/s Remember to include units in your answers! Modelling with Parametric Equations We can use parametric equations to model real life situations, such as: The motion of objects The shape of objects

resources.title: Modelling with Sequences & Series

content.topicNotes: Modelling with Sequences and Series We can use sequences and series to model numerical problems that occur in real life. Fixed amount Numbers that increase by fixed amounts can be modelled by arithmetic sequences. Example On the Sunday after a minor surgery, a woman is able to walk a half-mile. Each Sunday, she walks an additional quarter-mile. After 8 weeks, what will be the total number of miles she has walked? Arithmetic series The number of miles the woman walks increases by a fixed amount each week. This means we can model this as an arithmetic series with $$a_1 = 0.5$$ and $$d = 0.25$$. Using the equation for the sum of an arithmetic series, we have: $$S_8 = \frac{1}{2}n(2a_1 + (n-1)d) = \frac{8}{2}\times(2\times0.5 + 7\times0.25) = 11$$ So the woman has walked a total of 11 miles after her surgery. Fixed percentage Numbers that increase by a fixed percentage or fraction can be modelled by geometric sequences. Example A pendulum travels a distance of 48 cm on its first swing. On each successive swing, it travels $$\frac{3}{4}$$ of the distance of the previous swing. What is the total distance travelled by the pendulum when it stops swinging? Geometric series The distance of the swing decreases by a fixed fraction. That means we can model total distance of the pendulum as a geometric series with $$a = 48$$ and $$r=\frac{3}{4}$$. Since $$|r|<1$$, we know that the infinite series is convergent and that the pendulum's distance will diminish until it eventually stops. Finding the sum of the infinite series will give the total distance travelled by the pendulum. Sum of infinite series Using the equation for the sum of an infinite geometric series, we have: $$S_{\infty}=\frac{\small a}{\small 1-r}=\frac{\small 48}{\small 1-\frac{3}{4}} = \frac{\small 48}{\small \frac{1}{4}}=192$$ So the pendulum travels a total distance of 192 cm before it stops.

resources.title: Natural Logarithm

content.topicNotes: Natural Logarithms We often use a specific number as the base of our logarithms. The number e The number $$e$$ is an important irrational number in mathematics. The number $$e$$ can be defined as the base of an exponential function $$y=e^x$$ whose slope is equal to the function itself. The value of $$e$$ is approximately 2.71828. Natural logarithms Logarithms with base $$e$$ are called natural logarithms. Natural logarithms have their own notation: $$\log_e(x)=\ln(x)$$ They are defined as the inverse of the exponential function of base $$e$$: $$\ln(x) = y \Leftrightarrow e^y=x$$ Properties Natural logarithms follow the same inverse, product, quotient and power rules as other logarithms: $$\ln(2) + \ln(3) = \ln(6)$$ $$\ln(x^6)=6\ln(x)$$

resources.title: Notation in Mathematical Arguments

content.topicNotes: Notation in Mathematical Arguments When studying maths at a higher level, you need to be able to write mathematical arguments using the correct notation. Implies The implies symbol is a type of arrow written as $$\Rightarrow$$. We use this symbol to show when one equation implies that another equation is true. For example, $$x = 5$$ implies that $$x^2 = 25$$. So we can write $$x = 5 \Rightarrow x^2=25$$ Note that this relationship only goes one way, as $$x^2=25$$ does not imply that $$x=5$$ as it could also equal −5. Equivalence The double-ended arrow symbol $$\Leftrightarrow$$ is used to show when two equations are equivalent. This means that one equation being true implies the other is true, and vice versa. For example, $$x^2 - y^2 = 9 \Leftrightarrow (x+y)(x-y) = 9$$ Therefore The symbol for the word 'therefore' is ∴, which is a triangle of three dots. The symbol does not show a relation between equations, but is used as shorthand instead of writing out the word 'therefore'. For example, $$x = 2a$$, therefore $$x$$ is even. So we can write $$x = 2a$$ ∴ $$x$$ is even. Because The symbol for the word 'because' is ∵, which is an upside-down triangle of three dots. The symbol does not show a relation between equations, but is used as shorthand instead of writing out the word 'because'. For example, $$x^2 + 1 = 5$$ because $$x = 2$$. So we can write ∵ $$x=2,; x^2 +1=5$$

resources.title: Parametric Equations

content.topicNotes: What are Parametric Equations? Parametric equations define the coordinates of a graph as functions of a third variable, $$t$$. Each coordinate of the graph is given by the point $$(x=f(t),y=g(t))$$. Definition We can define a curve using the equations: $$x = f(t)$$ and $$y = g(t)$$ These are called parametric equations. Parametric equations define a point on the curve in terms of a parameter $$t$$. You must specify the domain of $$t$$ that the curve exists for when defining a curve parametrically. Example A curve has parametric equations: $$x = t-1,; y = 2t+4, ;-3\leq t \leq 2$$ By substituting in values of $$t$$ in the domain given, we can find the coordinates of points on the curve. Finding points on the curve For example, when $$t=-1$$: $$x = -1-1 = -2$$ $$y=(2\times -1) +4=2$$. Conversion If a curve is only in terms of the variables $$x$$ and $$y$$, we call this a Cartesian equation. We can convert parametric equations into a Cartesian equation by rearranging for $$t$$ and substituting it in. Example A curve has parametric equations: $$x = t-1,; y = 2t+4, ;-3\leq t \leq 2$$ Rearranging the first equation, we get: $$x = t-1 \rightarrow t = x+1$$ Substitute in $$t$$ Substituting this into the equation for $$y$$: $$y = 2(x+1)+4 = 2x+6$$ That means the Cartesian equation for this curve is $$y = 2x+6$$ However, we can't finish there, as the curve was specified for the region $$-3\leq t\leq2$$. Find the domain We need to substitute in for $$t$$ into the inequality that describes its domain: $$-3\leq x+1\leq2$$ Subtracting one from each side gives: $$-4\leq x\leq 1$$ Cartesian equation So the curve with parametric equations: $$x = t-1,; y = 2t+4, ;-3\leq t \leq 2$$ Is the same as the Cartesian equation: $$y = 2x+6, -4\leq x\leq1$$

resources.title: Partial Fractions - Practice

content.topicNotes: What are Partial Fractions? If an algebraic fraction has a numerator that is lower in degree than its denominator, we can split it up into partial fractions. This allows us to do calculations more easily. What are the linear factors in a denominator? To split up an algebraic fraction into its partial fractions, we need to factorise the denominator into its linear factors. For example, $$\frac{\small 11x-7}{\small 2x^3 -3x^2 -2x} \rightarrow \frac{\small 11x-7}{\small x(2x + 1)(x-2)}$$ Fractions with 2 linear factors If a fraction has a denominator consisting of 2 different linear factors, we can express it as the sum of partial fractions: For example, $$\frac{\small 11x-7}{\small (2x + 1)(x-2)} \equiv \frac{\small A}{\small 2x+1} + \frac{\small B}{\small x-2}$$ Where $$A$$ and $$B$$ are constants. These constants are found by adding the fractions and either substituting in values of $$x$$ or by equating coefficients of $$x$$. Fractions with 3 linear factors If a fraction has a denominator consisting of 3 different linear factors, we can express it as the sum of partial fractions. For example, $$\frac{\small 2x+4}{\small (x + 3)(3x+1)(x-2)} \equiv \frac{\small A}{\small x+3} + \frac{ \small B}{\small 3x+1}+\frac{\small C}{\small x-2}$$ Where $$A$$, $$B$$ and $$C$$ are constants to be found by substitution or equating coefficients. Fractions with repeated factors If a fraction has a denominator consisting of 2 different linear factors and one is repeated, we can express it as the sum of partial fractions: For example, $$\frac{5}{(x-1)(3x+2)^2} \equiv \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{3x+2} + \frac{C}{(3x+2)^2}$$ Where $$A$$, $$B$$ and $$C$$ are constants to be found by substitution or equating coefficients.

resources.title: Pascal's Triangle

content.topicNotes: What is Pascal's Triangle? Pascal's triangle is an arrangement of numbers that allow us to quickly work out the coefficients of terms when you expand expressions of the form $$(x+y)^n$$. How do you construct Pascal's triangle? To construct Pascal's triangle, we start by writing a 1. In the row below, we write two 1’s either side. For the third row, we add the two 1's in the second row to give 2, and write this in between them on the row below. The start and ending numbers of a row are always equal to 1. Pascal's triangle We continue this way, adding two numbers to find the number in the row below it until we have written out as many rows as we would like. Expanding binomials We can use the numbers in each row of a pascal triangle to expand expressions of the form $$(x+y)^n$$. The first row is equal to $$(x+y)^0$$. Expanding binomials The second row gives the coefficients of the terms of the $$(x+y)^1$$ expansion. The coefficients of the terms of the $$(x+y)^{n}$$ expansion are given by the $$(n+1)$$th row of Pascal's triangle. Expanding binomials Each term in the expansion has a total power that is equal to the power of the expansion. For example, $$(x+y)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2y^1+3y^2x^1 +y^3$$ Each term contains powers that add up to three. Example What is the expansion of $$(2x+3)^4$$? Write out Pascal's triangle up to row 5 The coefficients of the terms in the expansion $$(2x+3)^4$$ are given by the $$5$$th row of Pascal's triangle. Write out coefficients of expansion The coefficients are: $$1,4,6,4,1$$ Multiply coefficients Multiply each coefficient by decreasing orders of $$2x$$ and increasing orders of $$3$$: $$(2x)^43^0\rightarrow(2x)^33^1\rightarrow(2x)^23^2\rightarrow(2x)^13^2\rightarrow(2x)^03^4$$ Write the sum of the terms The answer is the sum of each term: $$(2x+3)^4 = (2x)^4 + 4(2x)^33^1 + 6(2x)^23^2+4(2x)^23^3 + 3^4$$ Answer We can simplify our answer by working out the powers: $$(2x+3)^4 = 16x^4+96x^3 + 216x^2 +216x + 81$$

resources.title: Polynomial Identities

content.topicNotes: Polynomial Identities An identity equation is true for all values of the variable. To prove an identity holds, show that the left-hand side equals the right-hand side. Example Show that $$(x^2 + y^2)^2 = (x^2-y^2)^2+(2xy)^2$$ Expand the left-hand side using FOIL Collect any like terms together. Add expression equivalent to zero Adding $$(-2x^2y^2+2x^2y^2)$$ does not change the expression as it is equal to zero. It allows us to combine the other terms in a way that resembles the right-hand side of the equation. Recombine The first, third and fourth term of the expression are the same as the expansion of $$(x^2-y^2)^2$$. By substituting different values of $$x$$ and $$y$$, we can use this identity to generate Pythagorean triples. 32 + 42 = 52 Full proof

resources.title: Polynomials

content.topicNotes: Polynomials You need to be able to name polynomials and give their degrees. Terminology When a term in an expression is of the form $$ax^m$$, where $$a$$ is a constant and $$m$$ is a whole number, it is called a monomial. For example, $$3x^5$$ is a monomial. Similarly, a binomial is the sum or difference of two monomials. $$2x + 6x^4$$ is a binomial. A trinomial is the sum or difference of three monomials. $$1 + 4x - 5x^2$$ is a trinomial. Polynomials The general term for the sums of monomials is polynomials. $$1-2x + 4x^2 -17x^5 + 3x^{12}$$ is a polynomial. Polynomials can always be written in the form: $$a_n x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+ ... + a_2x^2 + a_1x + a_0$$ Where $$a_i$$ are real numbers that we call coefficients. Degree The degree of a term is the exponent of its variable. The degree of a constant is 0, as any constant $$a = ax^0$$. The degree of a polynomial is the highest degree of all its terms. The degree of $$3x^3-5x+7$$ is $$3$$.

content.topicNotes: Growth Growth can be thought of as when something gets larger over time. This might be the population of a particular species, the amount of money in a bank account or the number of people using Seneca. Linear growth Linear growth is when something increases by a steady amount over set time periods. E.g. a cinema gets 100 extra visitors each month. If they have 200 visitors in month 1, they will get 300 visitors in month 2, 400 visitors in month 3, 500 visitors in month 4, etc. Exponential growth Exponential growth is when something increases by a multiplier (or percentage) over set time periods. E.g. the number of people playing Fortnite increases by 2× each month. If they have 200 users in month 1, they will get 400 users in month 2, 800 users in month 3, 1,600 users in month 4, etc. Exponential growth in bacteria Populations of bacteria can grow exponentially. This means the number of bacteria increases by a set multiplier over a given time period. Exponential growth in bacteria 2 The population of an example colony of bacteria starts at one. If the population of bacteria doubles every hour you'd get the exponential growth seen above.
